nameStory: This spider gets its name from its resemblance to harvestmen, those long-legged arachnids also called 'daddy longlegs' that belong to the order Opiliones. The scientific name 'opilionoides' literally means 'harvestmen-like,' reflecting how people often mistake these delicate cellar spiders for their more familiar cousins. It's a case of mistaken identity that happens so often, scientists built it right into the name!
description: The Opilion-like Cellar Spider is a delicate, pale spider that builds messy cobwebs in quiet corners of buildings and natural shelters. Like other cellar spiders, it has an small, oval body and extremely long, thin legs that seem almost too fragile to support it. These spiders are typically small, with bodies rarely exceeding a quarter-inch long, though their legs can span over an inch. They're most notable for their habit of vibrating rapidly in their webs when disturbed, creating a blur of motion that makes them nearly impossible to see clearly.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When threatened, rapidly vibrates or 'bounces' in its web so fast it becomes a blur, making the web shake violently - this defensive behavior is the easiest way to confirm you've found a cellar spider

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds loose, irregular cobwebs that feel sticky and messy to touch, usually strung across corners or between surfaces rather than the neat orb webs of garden spiders

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small oval body that looks almost pinched in the middle, with legs so thin they appear thread-like and can be 6-8 times longer than the body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body typically 3-6mm long (about the size of a pencil eraser), but leg span can reach 25-30mm, giving it a very gangly appearance

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally pale yellowish-brown to gray coloration with subtle darker markings on the abdomen that may appear as faint chevrons or spots

habitat: Found primarily in human-made structures like basements, cellars, garages, and barns throughout New England, where they prefer undisturbed corners with moderate humidity. They also occur in natural shelters such as caves, rock crevices, and under overhanging ledges where conditions remain stable. Look for them in areas that stay consistently cool and slightly damp, away from direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, beginning to mate and lay eggs in their webs. This is when you're most likely to spot egg sacs - small, round bundles the female carries in her jaws.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and numerous. Juveniles from spring eggs begin appearing, and you may find multiple generations in the same web area.
seasonality.fall: Mating continues and late-season egg laying occurs. Adults prepare for winter by seeking more protected locations, moving deeper into basements or more sheltered outdoor spots.
seasonality.winter: Adults become sluggish but remain active in heated buildings. In unheated spaces, they may enter a dormant state but can still be found alive in their webs during warm spells.

funFact: Despite their fragile appearance, cellar spiders are actually fierce predators that regularly catch and eat other spiders much larger than themselves, including house spiders and even small wolf spiders - they use their long legs to wrap up prey while staying safely out of reach of dangerous fangs!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with harvestmen (daddy longlegs), but harvestmen don't build webs, have their body segments fused together (no 'waist'), and don't do the characteristic vibrating behavior. Remember: if it's bouncing in a web, it's a cellar spider; if it's walking around web-free, it's probably a harvestman.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'daddy longlegs' causes endless confusion because it's used for harvestmen (Opiliones), cellar spiders (Pholcidae), and crane flies (insects) depending on where you live. In New England, most people call harvestmen 'daddy longlegs,' so calling these 'cellar spiders' helps avoid mix-ups at nature walks and family gatherings!
compareHints: Distinguishing this species from its close relative, the Long-bodied Cellar Spider, requires very close examination of body proportions and leg length ratios that are difficult to assess in the field. Both species behave identically and occupy similar habitats in New England buildings. For practical identification purposes, both can be considered part of the 'cellar spider complex' since they're nearly impossible to separate without microscopic examination.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Long-bodied Cellar Spiders are the most common cellar spider in New England homes and have the most extremely elongated body proportions.
Manuel's Cellar Spider is very similar to the Long-bodied Cellar Spider, and they're nearly impossible to tell apart without microscopic examination.
Compared to the common Long-bodied Cellar Spider, crypticolens is generally smaller and more pale in coloration.
